claims.source: Starvation-dependent modulation of navigation behaviors was observed only on thermal gradients; fed and starved animals exhibited similar velocities and dispersed throughout an isothermal plate held at 20°C (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by velocity measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: On spatial thermal gradients, negative thermotaxis is mediated primarily via klinokinesis.
claims.source: On spatial thermal gradients, negative thermotaxis is mediated primarily via klinokinesis (Clark et al., 2007; Luo et al., 2014a; Ryu and Samuel, 2002; Zariwala et al., 2003).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Clark et al., 2007; Luo et al., 2014a; Ryu and Samuel, 2002; Zariwala et al., 2003.

claims.claim: In klinokinesis, worms moving toward cooler temperatures suppress reorientations (turns) and consequently extend the duration of forward movement (runs).
claims.source: In this behavioral strategy, worms moving toward cooler temperatures suppress reorientations (turns) and consequently, extend the duration of forward movement (runs).
claims.evidence: This describes the klinokinesis behavioral strategy, supported by established knowledge in the field.

claims.claim: When moving toward the non-preferred warmer temperatures, worms increase turn frequency and decrease run duration.
claims.source: Conversely, when moving toward the non-preferred warmer temperatures, worms increase turn frequency and decrease run duration.
claims.evidence: This describes the klinokinesis behavioral strategy, supported by established knowledge in the field.

claims.claim: Following a turn, worms preferentially bias the direction of a new run toward cooler temperatures.
claims.source: In parallel, following a turn, worms preferentially bias the direction of a new run toward cooler temperatures (Luo et al., 2014a).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Luo et al., 2014a.

claims.claim: Well-fed animals exhibited robust negative thermotaxis bias on short thermal gradients.
claims.source: While well-fed animals exhibited robust negative thermotaxis bias under these conditions, animals starved for >2 hr were essentially athermotactic, indicating that these animals were unable to modulate turning frequency as a function of experienced temperature changes (Figure 1C; Chi et al., 2007; Hedgecock and Russell, 1975; Kodama et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by thermotaxis bias data shown in Figure 1C.

claims.claim: Animals starved for >2 hr were essentially athermotactic.
claims.source: While well-fed animals exhibited robust negative thermotaxis bias under these conditions, animals starved for >2 hr were essentially athermotactic, indicating that these animals were unable to modulate turning frequency as a function of experienced temperature changes (Figure 1C; Chi et al., 2007; Hedgecock and Russell, 1975; Kodama et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by thermotaxis bias data shown in Figure 1C and citations to Chi et al., 2007; Hedgecock and Russell, 1975; Kodama et al., 2006.

claims.claim: Starved animals failed to orient run direction toward cooler temperatures following a turn, and instead oriented their runs near-randomly on the gradient.
claims.source: We established that starved animals also failed to orient run direction toward cooler temperatures following a turn, and instead oriented their runs near-randomly on the gradient (Figure 1D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by orientation analysis shown in Figure 1D.

claims.claim: Average velocities of fed and starved animals were indistinguishable on short thermal gradients.
claims.source: Average velocities of fed and starved animals were indistinguishable on these gradients (average velocity: fed – 117 μm/s, starved for 3 hr – 106 μm/s; n = 10 animals each).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by velocity measurements reported in the text.

claims.claim: Prolonged starvation abolishes both klinokinesis and biased run direction to disrupt negative thermotaxis.
claims.source: Together, these observations indicate that prolonged starvation abolishes both klinokinesis and biased run direction to disrupt negative thermotaxis.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the behavioral data showing loss of both turning modulation and directional bias.

claims.claim: Refeeding starved animals for an hour was sufficient to restore robust negative thermotaxis bias.
claims.source: Refeeding starved animals for an hour was sufficient to restore robust negative thermotaxis bias (Figure 1C; Chi et al., 2007; Mohri et al., 2005)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by refeeding data shown in Figure 1C and citations to Chi et al., 2007; Mohri et al., 2005.

claims.claim: Prolonged starvation does not irreversibly alter the function of the thermotaxis circuit.
claims.source: Refeeding starved animals for an hour was sufficient to restore robust negative thermotaxis bias (Figure 1C; Chi et al., 2007; Mohri et al., 2005), indicating that prolonged starvation does not irreversibly alter the function of the underlying circuit.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the refeeding experiment showing reversibility of the starvation effect.

claims.claim: The presence of bacteria on the lids of agar plates did not override the effect of starvation on negative thermotaxis.
claims.source: However, the presence of bacteria on the lids of agar plates did not override the effect of starvation on negative thermotaxis (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: Feeding animals either live or antibiotic-killed bacteria was sufficient to mimic the well-fed condition for negative thermotaxis.
claims.source: Moreover, feeding animals either live or antibiotic-killed bacteria was sufficient to mimic the well-fed condition for negative thermotaxis (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: Prolonged starvation alters internal state to disrupt negative thermotaxis.
claims.source: We infer that prolonged starvation alters internal state to disrupt negative thermotaxis.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experiments showing that bacterial odors alone are insufficient and that feeding (live or dead bacteria) is necessary.

claims.claim: AFD responds to temperature changes above a Tc-determined threshold referred to as T*AFD.
claims.source: AFD responds to temperature changes above a Tc-determined threshold referred to as T*AFD (Clark et al., 2006; Kimura et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Clark et al., 2006; Kimura et al., 2004.

claims.claim: Temperature-driven calcium dynamics in AFD were largely indifferent to feeding state.
claims.source: Confirming and extending previous observations using different temperature stimulus paradigms (Biron et al., 2006; Matsuyama and Mori, 2020; Ramot et al., 2008a; Tsukada et al., 2016), we found that temperature-driven calcium dynamics in AFD were largely indifferent to feeding state, although we noted a small but statistically significant decrease in T*AFD upon starvation (Figure 1E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 1E and citations to Biron et al., 2006; Matsuyama and Mori, 2020; Ramot et al., 2008a; Tsukada et al., 2016.

claims.claim: There was a small but statistically significant decrease in T*AFD upon starvation.
claims.source: Confirming and extending previous observations using different temperature stimulus paradigms (Biron et al., 2006; Matsuyama and Mori, 2020; Ramot et al., 2008a; Tsukada et al., 2016), we found that temperature-driven calcium dynamics in AFD were largely indifferent to feeding state, although we noted a small but statistically significant decrease in T*AFD upon starvation (Figure 1E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by T*AFD measurements shown in Figure 1E.

claims.claim: The observed change in T*AFD is unlikely to drive starvation-induced loss of negative thermotaxis behavior.
claims.source: Since manipulations resulting in effects of a similar magnitude on T*AFD do not disrupt negative thermotaxis (Inada et al., 2006; Takeishi et al., 2016; Wasserman et al., 2011), we infer that the observed change in T*AFD is unlikely to drive starvation-induced loss of negative thermotaxis behavior.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on comparison with previous studies showing that similar magnitude changes in T*AFD do not affect thermotaxis.

claims.claim: Food deprivation has been suggested to alter the phase relationship between AFD and AIY temperature responses in a restricted temperature range.
claims.source: In a recent study, food deprivation has been suggested to alter the phase relationship between AFD and AIY temperature responses in a restricted temperature range and may mediate plasticity in positive thermotaxis (Matsuyama and Mori, 2020).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Matsuyama and Mori, 2020.

claims.claim: Stochastic calcium transients were observed in AIY neurons in response to a shallow linear temperature ramp.
claims.source: In contrast to the robust and deterministic temperature responses observed in AFD, we observed stochastic calcium transients in AIY neurons expressing GCaMP6s in immobilized animals in response to the shallow linear temperature ramp (Figure 1F) (also see Hawk et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 1F and citation to Hawk et al., 2018.

claims.claim: No significant differences in total response duration per neuron or the average duration of individual response bouts in AIY were observed between fed and starved animals.
claims.source: We observed no significant differences in total response duration per neuron or the average duration of individual response bouts in AIY between fed and starved animals (Figure 1G, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of AIY calcium imaging data shown in Figure 1G and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claims.claim: The proportion of AIY neurons responding to the rising temperature stimulus in the temperature range of the behavioral assay (23–28°C) was similar under fed and starved conditions.
claims.source: Moreover, the proportion of AIY neurons responding to the rising temperature stimulus in the temperature range of the behavioral assay (23–28°C) was similar under fed and starved conditions, although we noted that responses were initiated at a lower temperature in a subset of AIY neurons upon starvation (Figure 1F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of AIY calcium imaging data shown in Figure 1F.

claims.claim: Temperature responses in AIY can be driven by thermal inputs from sensory neurons other than AFD.
claims.source: Temperature responses in AIY can be driven by thermal inputs from sensory neurons other than AFD (Biron et al., 2008; Hawk et al., 2018; Kuhara et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Biron et al., 2008; Hawk et al., 2018; Kuhara et al., 2008.

claims.claim: The frequency of responses in AIY in the peri-Tc temperature range was similar in fed and starved animals.
claims.source: We found that the frequency of responses in this temperature range in AIY was also similar in fed and starved animals (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of AIY responses near Tc shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claims.claim: AFD thermosensory responses and likely AFD synaptic output as measured by responses in AIY are largely unaffected by starvation.
claims.source: We conclude that AFD thermosensory responses, and likely AFD synaptic output as measured by responses in AIY, are largely unaffected by starvation, and that alternate pathways incorporate internal state information elsewhere in the thermotaxis circuit.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the AFD and AIY imaging data showing minimal changes with starvation.

claims.claim: AWC responds robustly to food-related volatile odors.
claims.source: AWC responds robustly to food-related volatile odors (Bargmann et al., 1993; Chalasani et al., 2007)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bargmann et al., 1993; Chalasani et al., 2007.

claims.claim: AWC olfactory responses and AWC-driven behaviors are modulated by the presence or absence of bacterial food.
claims.source: AWC olfactory responses and AWC-driven behaviors are modulated by the presence or absence of bacterial food (Chalasani et al., 2010; Cho et al., 2016; Colbert and Bargmann, 1995; Lin et al., 2010; Neal et al., 2015; Torayama et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Chalasani et al., 2010; Cho et al., 2016; Colbert and Bargmann, 1995; Lin et al., 2010; Neal et al., 2015; Torayama et al., 2007.

claims.claim: Silencing AWC during the assay alone was sufficient to restore negative thermotaxis bias in starved animals.
claims.source: However, silencing AWC during the assay alone was sufficient to restore negative thermotaxis bias in starved animals (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by HisCl1-mediated silencing data shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: HisCl1-mediated silencing of AWC restored the ability of starved animals to bias the direction of runs following turns toward cooler temperatures.
claims.source: Moreover, HisCl1-mediated silencing of AWC restored the ability of starved animals to bias the direction of runs following turns toward cooler temperatures (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by orientation analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: Optogenetic silencing of AWC during the assay was sufficient to restore negative thermotaxis bias in starved animals.
claims.source: Optogenetic silencing of AWC during the assay was again sufficient to restore negative thermotaxis bias in starved animals (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by GtACR2-mediated silencing data shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: Acute silencing of AWC in adult animals is sufficient to abolish starvation-dependent thermotaxis behavioral plasticity.
claims.source: These results indicate that acute silencing of AWC in adult animals is sufficient to abolish starvation-dependent thermotaxis behavioral plasticity.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the AWC silencing experiments using both HisCl1 and GtACR2.

claims.claim: AWC activity is necessary during the execution of thermotaxis behavior to disrupt negative thermotaxis.
claims.source: Moreover, we infer that AWC activity is necessary during the execution of thermotaxis behavior to disrupt negative thermotaxis.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that silencing AWC only during the assay (not during starvation) is sufficient to restore thermotaxis.

claims.claim: AWC neurons in fed animals exhibited relatively infrequent and stochastic calcium transients in response to a shallow rising temperature stimulus from 23–28°C.
claims.source: AWC neurons in fed animals grown overnight at 20°C exhibited relatively infrequent and stochastic calcium transients in response to a shallow rising temperature stimulus from 23–28°C, the temperature range in which animals exhibit negative thermotaxis in our behavioral assays (see Materials and methods; Figure 2C; Biron et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 2C and citation to Biron et al., 2008.

claims.claim: The total response duration per neuron as well as the average duration of individual events in AWC was significantly increased in response to a rising temperature ramp upon starvation for 3 hr.
claims.source: However, we found that the total response duration per neuron as well as the average duration of individual events was significantly increased in response to a rising temperature ramp upon starvation for 3 hr (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging analysis shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claims.claim: A greater proportion of AWC neurons responded as the temperature increased in starved animals.
claims.source: Moreover, a greater proportion of AWC neurons responded as the temperature increased in starved animals (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: AWC neuronal responses were unaltered in starved animals held at 20°C.
claims.source: In contrast, AWC neuronal responses were unaltered in starved animals held at 20°C (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data at constant temperature shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claims.claim: Starvation increases responses to rising temperatures in AWC, and this increased activity is necessary to disrupt negative thermotaxis.
claims.source: Together, these results indicate that starvation increases responses to rising temperatures in AWC, and that this increased activity is necessary to disrupt negative thermotaxis.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the AWC imaging and silencing experiments.

claims.claim: Increasing AWC activity either via genetic or optogenetic means has been shown to promote reversals and turns via inhibition and activation of the postsynaptic primary layer interneurons AIY and AIA, and AIB, respectively.
claims.source: Increasing AWC activity either via genetic or optogenetic means has previously been shown to promote reversals and turns via inhibition and activation of the postsynaptic primary layer interneurons AIY and AIA, and AIB, respectively (Figure 3A; Albrecht and Bargmann, 2011; Chalasani et al., 2007; Chalasani et al., 2010; Gordus et al., 2015; Gray et al., 2005; White et al., 1986).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Albrecht and Bargmann, 2011; Chalasani et al., 2007; Chalasani et al., 2010; Gordus et al., 2015; Gray et al., 2005; White et al., 1986, and reference to Figure 3A showing circuit connectivity.

claims.claim: AIY and AIA inhibit reversals and/or turns.
claims.source: Consequently, AIY and AIA inhibit, and AIB promotes, reversals and/or turns (Figure 3A; Chalasani et al., 2007; Gordus et al., 2015; Gray et al., 2005; Kocabas et al., 2012; Li et al., 2014; López-Cruz et al., 2019; Tsalik and Hobert, 2003; Wakabayashi et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Chalasani et al., 2007; Gordus et al., 2015; Gray et al., 2005; Kocabas et al., 2012; Li et al., 2014; López-Cruz et al., 2019; Tsalik and Hobert, 2003; Wakabayashi et al., 2004, and reference to Figure 3A.

claims.claim: AIB promotes reversals and/or turns.
claims.source: Consequently, AIY and AIA inhibit, and AIB promotes, reversals and/or turns (Figure 3A; Chalasani et al., 2007; Gordus et al., 2015; Gray et al., 2005; Kocabas et al., 2012; Li et al., 2014; López-Cruz et al., 2019; Tsalik and Hobert, 2003; Wakabayashi et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Chalasani et al., 2007; Gordus et al., 2015; Gray et al., 2005; Kocabas et al., 2012; Li et al., 2014; López-Cruz et al., 2019; Tsalik and Hobert, 2003; Wakabayashi et al., 2004, and reference to Figure 3A.

claims.claim: AIA and AIB exhibited stochastic calcium transients in response to a shallow rising temperature stimulus in the T > Tc regime.
claims.source: Similar to AIY, both AIA and AIB exhibited stochastic calcium transients in response to a shallow rising temperature stimulus in the T > Tc regime (Figure 3B–C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 3B–C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: AIB temperature responses were similar in fed and starved animals.
claims.source: AIB temperature responses were similar in fed and starved animals (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: Responses to a rising temperature ramp in AIA were markedly altered upon starvation.
claims.source: However, responses to a rising temperature ramp in AIA were markedly altered upon starvation (Figure 3B–C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 3B–C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: AIA appeared to be tonically active and exhibited frequent calcium transients in fed animals subjected to either a rising temperature stimulus or a constant holding temperature of 20°C.
claims.source: AIA appeared to be tonically active and exhibited frequent calcium transients in fed animals subjected to either a rising temperature stimulus or a constant holding temperature of 20°C (Figure 3B–C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B–C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 3B–C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B–C.

claims.claim: Upon prolonged starvation, the proportion of responding animals, the total response duration per neuron as well as the average duration of individual response bouts in AIA were significantly suppressed in response to a rising temperature ramp but not when held at 20°C.
claims.source: However, upon prolonged starvation, the proportion of responding animals, the total response duration per neuron as well as the average duration of individual response bouts were significantly suppressed in response to a rising temperature ramp but not when held at 20°C (Figure 3B–C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B–C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging analysis shown in Figure 3B–C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B–C.

claims.claim: Temperature responses in AIZ exhibited tonic stochastic activity in fed animals subjected to a rising temperature stimulus, and these responses were decreased upon starvation.
claims.source: Under our imaging conditions, temperature responses in AIZ, like those in AIA, exhibited tonic stochastic activity in fed animals subjected to a rising temperature stimulus, and these responses were decreased upon starvation (Figure 3D–E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 3D–E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claims.claim: Acute inhibition of the AIA circuit via addition of histamine to the assay plate resulted in animals exhibiting extensive reversals and turns at the starting temperature regardless of feeding state.
claims.source: However, acute inhibition of the AIA circuit via addition of histamine to the assay plate resulted in animals exhibiting extensive reversals and turns at the starting temperature regardless of feeding state, and consequent inability of these animals to navigate the gradient (Figure 3F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data with HisCl1-mediated AIA inhibition shown in Figure 3F.

claims.claim: Acute inhibition of AIZ via expression of HisCl1 and addition of histamine decreased spontaneous reversals on an isothermal plate.
claims.source: However, although acute inhibition of AIZ via expression of HisCl1 (see Materials and methods) and addition of histamine decreased spontaneous reversals on an isothermal plate as reported previously (Gray et al., 2005; Li et al., 2014; Tsalik and Hobert, 2003; Figure 3—figure supplement 1F), AIZ inhibition had no effect on the expected thermotaxis behavior of either fed or starved animals (Figure 3G).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by reversal frequency data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1F and citations to Gray et al., 2005; Li et al., 2014; Tsalik and Hobert, 2003.

claims.claim: AIZ inhibition had no effect on the expected thermotaxis behavior of either fed or starved animals.
claims.source: However, although acute inhibition of AIZ via expression of HisCl1 (see Materials and methods) and addition of histamine decreased spontaneous reversals on an isothermal plate as reported previously (Gray et al., 2005; Li et al., 2014; Tsalik and Hobert, 2003; Figure 3—figure supplement 1F), AIZ inhibition had no effect on the expected thermotaxis behavior of either fed or starved animals (Figure 3G).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by thermotaxis bias data shown in Figure 3G.

claims.claim: While starvation inhibits activity in both AIA and AIZ, complete suppression of these responses in AIA but not AIZ disrupts negative thermotaxis regardless of feeding state.
claims.source: We conclude that while starvation inhibits activity in both AIA and AIZ, complete suppression of these responses in AIA but not AIZ disrupts negative thermotaxis regardless of feeding state.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the imaging and manipulation experiments on AIA and AIZ.

claims.claim: Activation of AIA was sufficient to restore the ability of starved animals to perform negative thermotaxis.
claims.source: Activation of AIA was sufficient to restore the ability of starved animals to perform negative thermotaxis (Figure 3H).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by optogenetic activation data shown in Figure 3H.

claims.claim: AWC inhibits AIA via glutamatergic signaling.
claims.source: AWC inhibits AIA via glutamatergic signaling (Chalasani et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Chalasani et al., 2010.

claims.claim: Knocking out the glutamate transporter eat-4 cell-specifically in AWC resulted in robust negative thermotaxis behavior by starved animals.
claims.source: Indeed, we found that knocking out the glutamate transporter eat-4 cell-specifically in AWC (López-Cruz et al., 2019) resulted in robust negative thermotaxis behavior by starved animals (Figure 3I).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data with AWC-specific eat-4 knockout shown in Figure 3I and citation to López-Cruz et al., 2019.

claims.claim: Upon prolonged starvation, increased AWC temperature responses inhibit AIA via glutamatergic signaling to disrupt negative thermotaxis via warming-uncorrelated regulation of reversals and turns.
claims.source: These experiments suggest that upon prolonged starvation, increased AWC temperature responses inhibit AIA via glutamatergic signaling to disrupt negative thermotaxis via warming-uncorrelated regulation of reversals and turns.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the AWC and AIA manipulation and imaging experiments.

claims.claim: Suppression or activation of AIA in fed or starved animals is sufficient to permit or inhibit negative thermotaxis, respectively.
claims.source: Moreover, these observations indicate that suppression or activation of AIA in fed or starved animals is sufficient to permit or inhibit negative thermotaxis, respectively.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the AIA manipulation experiments.

claims.claim: ins-1 has been shown to be expressed in multiple neuron types, including AIA as well as in the intestine.
claims.source: ins-1 has previously been shown to be expressed in multiple neuron types, including AIA as well as in the intestine, as assessed via GFP reporter expression under ins-1 regulatory sequences (Kodama et al., 2006; Pierce et al., 2001; Tomioka et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Kodama et al., 2006; Pierce et al., 2001; Tomioka et al., 2006.

claims.claim: Knocking out ins-1 in all or a majority of ins-1-expressing cells restored negative thermotaxis in starved animals.
claims.source: Knocking out ins-1 in all or a majority of ins-1-expressing cells by driving Cre::SL2::GFP under endogenous ins-1 regulatory sequences restored negative thermotaxis in starved animals, similar to the behavior of ins-1 null mutants (Figure 4A and D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by cell-specific knockout data shown in Figure 4A and D.

claims.claim: Animals in which ins-1 was deleted only in AIA or AIZ/AIB failed to perform negative thermotaxis upon starvation.
claims.source: However, animals in which ins-1 was deleted only in AIA or AIZ/AIB via Cre::SL2::GFP expression under the gcy-28d or odr-2b(3a) promoters, respectively failed to perform negative thermotaxis upon starvation.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by cell-specific knockout data shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: Knocking out ins-1 specifically in the intestine was sufficient to rescue the negative thermotaxis behavioral defect in starved animals.
claims.source: In contrast, knocking out ins-1 specifically in the intestine via Cre::SL2::GFP driven under the ifb-2 promoter was again sufficient to rescue the negative thermotaxis behavioral defect in starved animals (Figure 4A; Kodama et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by intestine-specific knockout data shown in Figure 4A and citation to Kodama et al., 2006.

claims.claim: ins-1 production from the intestine is necessary for starvation-mediated plasticity in negative thermotaxis.
claims.source: These results indicate that ins-1 production from the intestine is necessary for starvation-mediated plasticity in negative thermotaxis.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the cell-specific knockout experiments.

claims.claim: Levels of ins-1p::GFP::PEST expression in the gut were not altered upon food deprivation for 3 hr.
claims.source: However, levels of ins-1p::GFP::PEST expression in the gut were not altered upon food deprivation for 3 hr (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence quantification shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: Animals mutant for the age-1 and akt-1 kinases exhibited phenotypes similar to those of wild-type animals, such that they failed to perform negative thermotaxis upon starvation.
claims.source: We found that animals mutant for the age-1 and akt-1 kinases in this pathway exhibited phenotypes similar to those of wild-type animals, such that they failed to perform negative thermotaxis upon starvation (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claims.claim: Loss of function of the daf-18 PTEN phosphatase and daf-16 FOXO restored the ability of starved animals to perform negative thermotaxis.
claims.source: In contrast, loss of function of the daf-18 PTEN phosphatase and daf-16 FOXO restored the ability of starved animals to perform negative thermotaxis, similar to the phenotype of ins-1 mutants (Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: Starvation inhibits the ILP signaling pathway and phosphorylation of DAF-16 to disrupt negative thermotaxis.
claims.source: These observations imply that starvation inhibits the ILP signaling pathway and phosphorylation of DAF-16 to disrupt negative thermotaxis (Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the genetic analysis of the insulin signaling pathway components.

claims.claim: Loss of daf-2 function did not further affect starvation-mediated loss of negative thermotaxis.
claims.source: Consistent with the notion that DAF-2-mediated signaling is inhibited upon starvation, loss of daf-2 function did not further affect starvation-mediated loss of negative thermotaxis (Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: Upon starvation, INS-1 directly or indirectly antagonizes DAF-2 and disrupts negative thermotaxis via DAF-16.
claims.source: We infer that upon starvation, INS-1 directly or indirectly antagonizes DAF-2 and disrupts negative thermotaxis via DAF-16.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the genetic analysis of the insulin signaling pathway.

claims.claim: Addition of auxin during the 3 hr starvation period and the assay but not during the assay alone resulted in significant rescue of negative thermotaxis behavior upon DAF-16 depletion in AWC.
claims.source: We found that addition of auxin during the 3 hr starvation period and the assay but not during the assay alone resulted in significant rescue of negative thermotaxis behavior (Figure 4E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by auxin-induced degradation data shown in Figure 4E.

claims.claim: INS-1 targets DAF-16 in AWC to modulate negative thermotaxis bias as a function of feeding state.
claims.source: We infer that INS-1 targets DAF-16 in AWC to modulate negative thermotaxis bias as a function of feeding state, and that DAF-16 function is necessary during prolonged starvation for this modulation.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the AWC-specific DAF-16 depletion experiments.

claims.claim: DAF-16 function is necessary during prolonged starvation for modulation of negative thermotaxis.
claims.source: We infer that INS-1 targets DAF-16 in AWC to modulate negative thermotaxis bias as a function of feeding state, and that DAF-16 function is necessary during prolonged starvation for this modulation.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the timing of auxin addition in the DAF-16 depletion experiments.

claims.claim: In contrast to the increased activity in AWC observed in starved wild-type animals, temperature responses in AWC were no longer modulated by feeding state in ins-1 mutants.
claims.source: Indeed, we found that in contrast to the increased activity in AWC observed in starved wild-type animals, temperature responses in this neuron type were no longer modulated by feeding state in ins-1 mutants (Figure 4F and H, Figure 4—figure supplement 2E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data in ins-1 mutants shown in Figure 4F and H, and Figure 4—figure supplement 2E.

claims.claim: AWC neurons in both fed and starved ins-1 mutants exhibited infrequent responses similar to the response profiles of fed wild-type animals.

results.result: C. elegans exhibits thermotaxis behavior where well-fed animals navigate toward their cultivation temperature (Tc), mediated primarily by AFD sensory neurons and AIY interneurons, with AWC neurons playing a minor role. Temperature responses in AFD are indifferent to feeding state.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C4 establish the baseline thermotaxis circuit and prior knowledge. All claims are supported by appropriate citations to established literature (Hedgecock and Russell 1975, Mori and Ohshima 1995, Biron et al. 2006-2008). This provides the necessary context for the current work.

results.result: Prolonged food deprivation (3 hr) disrupts both negative and positive thermotaxis navigation behaviors. Starved animals exhibit increased turns and reversals, fail to modulate turning frequency (athermotactic), and fail to orient runs toward preferred temperatures, while maintaining normal velocity.
results.evaluation: Claims C14-C28 are well-supported by behavioral tracking data in Figure 1B-D showing disrupted navigation, increased turns/reversals, loss of thermotaxis bias, and random orientation following turns. The specificity to thermal gradients (C18-C19) and velocity measurements (C27) provide important controls. Statistical significance is demonstrated in Figure 1C.

results.result: Starvation-induced disruption of thermotaxis is reversible by refeeding and requires altered internal metabolic state rather than bacterial odor cues. Refeeding for 1 hour restores negative thermotaxis, and feeding with either live or dead bacteria is sufficient.
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C33 are supported by refeeding experiments (Figure 1C), bacterial odor exposure controls (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), and live vs. dead bacteria experiments (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C). The data convincingly demonstrate reversibility and rule out olfactory cues as the primary mechanism.

results.result: AFD thermosensory responses and AIY interneuron temperature responses are largely unaffected by starvation. While a small decrease in T*AFD was observed upon starvation, this change is unlikely to drive behavioral plasticity based on comparison with prior studies.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C44 are supported by calcium imaging data in Figure 1E-G and Figure 1—figure supplement 2. The small but statistically significant decrease in T*AFD (C36) is appropriately contextualized with citations showing similar magnitude changes don't affect thermotaxis (C37). AIY response metrics show no significant differences between fed and starved conditions.

results.result: Acute silencing of AWC neurons during the behavioral assay is sufficient to restore negative thermotaxis in starved animals. AWC activity is necessary during execution of thermotaxis behavior to disrupt negative thermotaxis, but not during the starvation period itself.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C51 are strongly supported by both HisCl1-mediated silencing (Figure 2A) and optogenetic silencing with GtACR2 (Figure 2B). The timing experiments showing silencing is only required during the assay (not during starvation) provide critical mechanistic insight. Controls with ASI silencing (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C) and chemotaxis assays confirm specificity.

results.result: Starvation significantly increases temperature responses in AWC neurons. Upon starvation, AWC exhibits increased total response duration, longer individual events, and greater proportion of responding neurons to rising temperature (23-28°C), but not at constant 20°C.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C56 are well-supported by calcium imaging data in Figure 2C-D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D. The specificity to rising temperature vs. constant temperature (C55) is an important control. Statistical significance is demonstrated by Kolmogorov-Smirnov test comparing cumulative distributions.

results.result: AIA interneurons exhibit tonic activity in fed animals that is significantly suppressed upon starvation in response to rising temperature but not at constant 20°C. AIB temperature responses are unaffected by starvation.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C64 are supported by calcium imaging data in Figure 3B-C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A-C. The differential effects on AIA vs. AIB, and the specificity to rising temperature provide important mechanistic insights. Statistical analyses using Kolmogorov-Smirnov tests and Mann-Whitney U tests are appropriate.

results.result: Complete suppression of AIA activity disrupts negative thermotaxis regardless of feeding state, while AIZ inhibition has no effect on thermotaxis behavior despite decreasing spontaneous reversals. Starvation inhibits activity in both AIA and AIZ, but only AIA suppression affects thermotaxis.
results.evaluation: Claims C66-C69 are supported by HisCl1-mediated inhibition experiments in Figure 3F-G and Figure 3—figure supplement 1F. The differential effects of AIA vs. AIZ inhibition provide important circuit-level insights. The observation that AIA inhibition prevents navigation in both fed and starved animals is well-documented.

results.result: Optogenetic activation of AIA restores negative thermotaxis in starved animals. AWC inhibits AIA via glutamatergic signaling, and cell-specific knockout of the glutamate transporter eat-4 in AWC restores thermotaxis in starved animals. AIA activity state is sufficient to gate thermotaxis behavior.
results.evaluation: Claims C70-C74 are supported by optogenetic activation (Figure 3H) and cell-specific eat-4 knockout experiments (Figure 3I). The glutamatergic mechanism is supported by citation to Chalasani et al. 2010 (C71). The sufficiency experiments provide strong causal evidence for the AWC→AIA pathway.

results.result: INS-1 production from the intestine is necessary for starvation-mediated plasticity in negative thermotaxis. Cell-specific knockout of ins-1 in the intestine, but not in AIA or AIZ/AIB, rescues thermotaxis behavior in starved animals.
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C79 are supported by Cre-Lox-mediated cell-specific knockout experiments in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-B. The specificity of intestinal vs. neuronal ins-1 is well-demonstrated. The recombination reporter controls (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B) validate the cell-specificity of the manipulations.

results.result: Starvation inhibits the insulin signaling pathway through DAF-16/FOXO to disrupt thermotaxis. Loss of daf-18 PTEN or daf-16 FOXO restores thermotaxis in starved animals, while age-1 and akt-1 mutants behave like wild-type. INS-1 antagonizes DAF-2 signaling via DAF-16.
results.evaluation: Claims C80-C85 are supported by genetic analysis in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 2A. The epistasis analysis is logically sound and consistent with the canonical insulin signaling pathway (Figure 4C). The observation that ins-1 expression levels don't change (C80, Figure 4—figure supplement 1C) suggests post-transcriptional regulation.

results.result: INS-1 targets DAF-16 in AWC neurons to modulate thermotaxis as a function of feeding state. Auxin-induced degradation of DAF-16 specifically in AWC during starvation (but not during assay alone) rescues thermotaxis behavior.
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C88 are supported by auxin-induced degradation experiments in Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 2B. The timing requirement (degradation during starvation, not just during assay) provides important mechanistic insight. Controls with ASI-specific degradation (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C) demonstrate cell-specificity.

results.result: In ins-1 mutants, AWC and AIA temperature responses are no longer modulated by feeding state. Both fed and starved ins-1 mutants exhibit response profiles similar to fed wild-type animals, indicating INS-1 signaling is required for starvation-induced changes in neuronal activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C89-C92 are supported by calcium imaging in ins-1 mutants shown in Figure 4F-H and Figure 4—figure supplement 2E-F. The loss of feeding state modulation in ins-1 mutants provides strong genetic evidence linking INS-1 to the observed neuronal plasticity. Statistical comparisons are appropriate.

results.result: Feeding state alters thermotaxis behavior by engaging a modulatory AWC-AIA circuit that gates the output of the core AFD-AIY thermotaxis network. During starvation, INS-1 signaling from the gut acts via DAF-16 in AWC to enhance temperature responses, leading to glutamatergic inhibition of AIA and disruption of AFD-driven thermotaxis.
results.evaluation: Claims C6-C13 and C93-C99 represent the main conclusions of the paper, synthesizing results from behavioral, imaging, optogenetic, and genetic experiments. The model is well-supported by the collective evidence from Figures 1-4. The gating mechanism is demonstrated by sufficiency experiments (AWC silencing, AIA activation) and necessity experiments (genetic manipulations). The gut-to-brain signaling pathway is established through cell-specific knockouts.

results.result: Additional observations on temperature responses in AIY and AIZ. AIY exhibits stochastic calcium transients, can receive inputs from multiple sensory neurons, and shows similar peri-Tc response frequency in fed and starved animals. AIZ responses decrease upon starvation.
results.evaluation: Claims C38, C39, C42, and C65 provide supporting observations. C38 cites recent work on AFD-AIY phase relationships. C39 and C42 describe AIY response properties with appropriate citations. C65 documents AIZ responses. All are supported by imaging data in Figure 1F, Figure 3D-E, and appropriate citations.

results.result: Negative thermotaxis on spatial gradients is mediated via klinokinesis, where worms suppress turns and extend runs when moving toward preferred temperatures, and increase turn frequency when moving toward non-preferred temperatures. Worms also bias run direction toward cooler temperatures following turns.
results.evaluation: Claims C20-C23 describe established behavioral strategies with appropriate citations (Clark et al. 2007, Luo et al. 2014a, Ryu and Samuel 2002, Zariwala et al. 2003). These provide necessary background for interpreting the behavioral defects observed in starved animals.

results.result: Prior work has established that AWC responds to food-related odors and is modulated by feeding state. AWC inhibits AIY and AIA while activating AIB to promote turns/reversals. AWC inhibits AIA via glutamatergic signaling. ins-1 is expressed in multiple neuron types including AIA and in the intestine.
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C46, C57-C59, C71, and C75 summarize relevant prior work with appropriate citations. These establish the circuit connectivity (Figure 3A) and molecular mechanisms that form the basis for the current study's hypotheses and interpretations.

results.result: Prior studies have implicated INS-1 and insulin signaling in thermotaxis plasticity, shown starvation enhances AWC odorant responses, demonstrated ins-1 expression in AIA is sufficient for chemosensory modulation, and established principles of circuit degeneracy and neuromodulation in C. elegans and other systems.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C100, C103-C104, C106, C108-C110, C113, C115, C117, C119, C121, and C124 cite relevant prior literature that motivates and contextualizes the current work. All citations appear appropriate and accurately represent the cited work based on the descriptions provided.

results.result: The authors speculate that starvation-dependent changes in AWC allow prioritization of food-seeking over thermoregulation, that INS-1 may act via altered processing/release, that distinct pathways may modulate AWC under different conditions, that AIZ may function in degenerate circuits, and that modulatory gating mechanisms provide behavioral flexibility. They suggest these principles may generalize across sensory circuits.
results.evaluation: Claims C101-C102, C105, C107, C111-C112, C114, C116, C120, C122-C123, C125-C126 are explicitly labeled as speculations in the Discussion. While these are reasonable interpretations and hypotheses based on the data, they represent future directions rather than demonstrated results. The speculations are appropriately qualified and grounded in the experimental findings.

results.result: Acute inhibition of AWC and activation of AIA restores thermotaxis in starved animals, indicating the core thermotaxis circuit functions are maintained but masked by AWC-AIA activity state.
results.evaluation: Claim C118 synthesizes results from the manipulation experiments (Figures 2-3) and is well-supported by the sufficiency of AWC silencing and AIA activation to restore behavior. This demonstrates the gating mechanism where the modulatory circuit masks rather than disrupts the core circuit.
